How to Understand this Amritras

Amrit Ras — the essence, distilled. This book is the essence of The Complete Question Bank: the same every MTP/RTP/PYQ question, chapter by chapter, but stripped down to just its coordinates and its insight — no question text, no worked answer. It exists for the days when you already know how to solve a question, and just need to be reminded that it was asked, where it sits, and what usually goes wrong with it.

Use it this way: practise from the full Question Bank Book (or your class notes) first. In the last stretch before your exam, flip through this Amritras chapter by chapter — if a card's Q.No and topic bring the question straight back to mind, tick it off; if it doesn't, that's exactly what your Self Notes space and this chapter's own Error Register are for. For the complete book with the full question and worked answer, visit vcgurukul.com.

Colour key

Examiner’s Comment Author’s Note Flagged / Unverified

  • Examiner’s Comment (tan/orange) is a real quote from ICAI’s own published "Examiner’s Comments on the Performance of the Examinees" — ICAI’s own words.
  • Author’s Note (pale pink) is the author’s own identification of a likely pitfall where no real ICAI comment exists for that question — informed guidance, not an official finding, and may not apply in every case.
  • A flagged card (reddish border) means one detail on that question has not been independently re-verified with full confidence.

What's on every card

  • Source line — sitting, question number, and marks, so you know exactly which paper and how much it was worth.
  • Topic tag — the exact sub-topic within the chapter, so you know precisely where to go back and re-read if a card doesn't ring a bell.
  • Examiner's Comment / Author's Note — the one line of insight worth carrying into the exam hall.
  • Student Self Notes — three blank lines (one more than the main book) for your own reminder on this specific question.
  • My NB Page No / My Tag / Revision Phase — identical to the main book: where you worked this by hand, your own freeform triage word, and three tick-boxes for successive revision passes.

Topic-wise Marks Mapping

Every chapter opens with the same Topic-wise Marks Mapping table as the main book — which sub-topic was tested for how many marks, in which sitting, split by MTP / PYQ / RTP. Read this first: it tells you which part of the chapter to revise hardest.

Sanjeevani Booti — the Error Register (one page per chapter, this time)

Unlike the main book's single shared register at the back, Amritras gives each chapter its own one-page register — "Concepts I Forgot" and "Mistakes I Repeated More Than Twice" — right after that chapter's cards, so you log a mistake the moment it happens while revising that chapter, not thirty chapters later.

A few honest notes on these numbers

  • Each MTP/PYQ sitting's questions sum to 114 marks, not the paper's nominal 100 — Part II offers “answer any N of the remaining M”, and this book deliberately includes every optional question shown so you can practise all of them, not only the subset one particular sitting required.
  • RTP sittings contribute 0 marks to the total above — ICAI's own RTP documents are published without a marks-weighted answer key, not a gap in this book's tagging.
  • 763 of this edition's Common-Student-Mistakes notes are the author's own synthesized guidance (clearly labelled “Author's Note” wherever they appear), because a real ICAI Examiner's Comment document doesn't exist for every sitting yet.

Author’s Note: A common error is treating every difference between Ind AS and IFRS as a "carve-out", without recognising that removal of an option available under IFRS is explicitly not treated as a carve-out under the Ind AS framework.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure Framework)

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Author’s Note: A common gap is omitting income and expense from the list of financial statement elements, discussing only assets, liabilities and equity.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
Author’s Note: A common error is confusing neutrality with conservatism/prudence, treating a deliberately cautious understatement of results as still "neutral" when it is in fact a form of bias in the opposite direction.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP May 2023 Set 1 · Q6(d) · Marks: 5 · Topic 5: Objectives & Users of Fin Stmts  +  Topic 6: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions  +  Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts  +  Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Author’s Note: A common error is confusing the four qualitative characteristics (Understandability, Relevance, Reliability, Comparability) with the three fundamental accounting assumptions (Going Concern, Accrual, Consistency), or listing "Materiality"/"Prudence" as standalone qualitative characteristics rather than as components nested within Relevance and Reliability respectively.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
Author’s Note: A common error is naming only two or three of the four characteristics, or confusing "Reliability" (freedom from material error/bias) with "Relevance" (capacity to influence economic decisions) – the two are frequently swapped in a rushed answer.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
Author’s Note: A common error here is conflating neutrality with the separate qualitative characteristic of comparability, or answering only that neutrality is one of several sub-elements of reliability without explaining what makes information biased (i.e. selective presentation shifting the analytical conclusion).
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Author’s Note: A common error here is recording the ₹40,000 gain on settling ₹1,40,000 of creditors for ₹1,00,000 cash as if only the cash paid affects the position, instead of recognising that the ₹40,000 difference is a gain that increases equity while the full liability is extinguished.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP May 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 7/9/11: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts / Elements of Financial Statements / Capital Maintenance
Author’s Note: A common error in the capital-maintenance calculation is treating the ₹36,00,000 closing sale proceeds entirely as profit available for withdrawal, without first setting aside the ₹24,00,000 needed to restore the opening capital before any surplus can be withdrawn.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP May 2026 Set 2 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 7/9/11: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts / Elements of Financial Statements / Capital Maintenance
Author’s Note: Some examinees computed permissible drawings as the full closing cash balance of ₹36,00,000 rather than the excess over opening equity needed to keep capital intact, overstating the withdrawable amount.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP November 2023 Set 1 · Q6(c) · Marks: 5 · Topic 11: Capital Maintenance
Author’s Note: A common error is computing retained profit as historical sale proceeds less historical cost of goods sold (a financial-capital-maintenance answer) instead of restating the opening stock to its current replacement cost and comparing that against the closing cash balance, which is what the physical-capital-maintenance concept specifically requires.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q6(d) · Marks: 4 · Topic 10: Meas of Elements of Fin Stmts
Author’s Note: A common error is confusing Current Cost with Realisable Value – both involve a “current” amount, but Current Cost is the cost to acquire an equivalent asset today while Realisable Value is the amount obtainable by selling the existing asset today, a distinction the Framework treats as two genuinely separate bases.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP September 2024 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Topic 6: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions
Author’s Note: A common error is continuing to amortise the deferred expenses over their normal 5-year period and depreciate fixed assets on the usual straight-line basis, instead of writing off the deferred expenses immediately and depreciating fixed assets down to their net realisable value once the going concern assumption is dropped.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP September 2025 Set 1 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 1] · Marks: 4 · Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
Author’s Note: A common error here is describing the five elements in generic terms instead of reproducing the Framework's precise formal definitions, particularly the distinction between an asset's control (not necessarily ownership) and its expected future economic benefit.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
PYQ May 2023 · Q6(d) · Marks: 5 · Topic 11: Capital Maintenance
Author’s Note: Some examinees applied the closing price index to the opening equity when computing capital maintenance at current purchasing power, instead of correctly restating the historical opening capital to year-end purchasing power terms using the ratio of closing to opening index. A few also confused physical capital maintenance, which values opening equity at the year-end replacement cost per unit, with financial capital maintenance at current purchasing power, producing the wrong maximum-drawing figure for one or both bases.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
PYQ September 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Topic 1.2: The five key elements - assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses
Author’s Note: A direct theory recall question; common gaps include omitting the equity definition's distinction from liabilities, or failing to note that losses (unlike ordinary expenses) may fall outside the enterprise's normal activities.
Student Self Notes:

Author’s Note: A common error is comparing raw material's own cost against its own replacement cost in isolation, instead of first checking whether the finished product it converts into (Product P) will sell below its own total cost – AS 2 only permits marking raw material down to replacement cost when that downstream test fails. It is also easy to compute net selling price by forgetting the 5% brokerage deduction, which changes both the partly-finished-goods NRV and the finished-goods valuation.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q1(c) · Marks: 4 · Topic 7.7: Impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and value in use)
Author’s Note: A common error is using net selling price or value in use alone instead of the HIGHER of the two as the recoverable amount, or crediting the impairment loss against a revaluation reserve balance that does not exist here (the earlier downward revaluation was already charged to profit and loss, leaving no reserve to absorb the fresh impairment loss).

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the entire impairment loss as a straight debit to the Profit and Loss Account without first checking for, and setting off against, any remaining balance in the Revaluation Reserve relating to the same asset — only the loss in excess of that reserve balance should reach the Profit and Loss Account.

Author’s Note: Many examinees debited the entire ₹3,50,000 impairment loss to the profit and loss account, not applying AS 28's requirement (para 58) to first set off an impairment loss on a revalued asset against the remaining balance in that asset's revaluation reserve before charging the balance to P&L. Several also capitalised the ₹10,800 delay-related expenses instead of expensing them, since the asset was already ready for use on 1st October, 2022.

Author’s Note: A common error is failing to distinguish the treatment of the two legal actions — provisioning is required for the probable, reliably estimable outflow to customer K under AS 29, while the claim against supplier F, however probable, remains an unrecognisable contingent asset until its realisation is virtually certain, not merely highly probable.

I. Descriptive & Scenario-Based Questions (pure AS 4)

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q1(a) · Marks: 7 · Topic 1.4: Adjusting versus non-adjusting events after the balance sheet date, across five distinct fact patterns  +  Topic 2.2: Extraordinary item discovered after financial statements are approved, treated in the subsequent period
Author’s Note: A common error is treating all five items uniformly as either "always adjust" or "always disclose only", rather than separately testing each event against AS 4's adjusting-versus-non-adjusting distinction on its own facts — in particular, confusing the Court's post-year-end decision (an adjusting event, since it relates to a liability that already existed and was already provided for at the balance sheet date) with the cashier's embezzlement discovered after the accounts were approved (a subsequent-period item under AS 5, not an adjustment to the year already closed).

Author’s Note: A common error is treating any change in the basis of a provision estimate as automatically a change in accounting policy requiring restatement, without distinguishing a genuine policy change from a change in accounting estimate (moving to a more prudent estimation method for an existing policy of providing for non-moving inventory).

Author’s Note: A common error is treating the reversal of a no-longer-required provision as a prior period item merely because the original provision was created in an earlier year, missing AS 5's requirement that prior period items arise specifically from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements — a provision correctly created and later found unnecessary due to a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item, not a prior period correction.

PYQ May 2023 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Topic 3.3/3.4: Measurement of a foreign-currency monetary payable at the transaction/settlement exchange rate, compared under two settlement options
Author’s Note: A significant number of examinees omitted the notional borrowing cost of paying immediately (interest on funds foregone at the company's own 15% p.a. rate) when comparing the two options, effectively comparing only the cash discount against the deferred interest without placing both options on a common date. This led many to conclude that immediate payment was cheaper, missing that Trower Limited's own high borrowing rate outweighs the 1% cash discount once time value is properly reflected.

PYQ May 2026 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Topic 3.13: Para 46A option - exchange difference on foreign-currency loan capitalised to a depreciable asset, or accumulated in FCMITD if not asset-linked
Author’s Note: Many examinees applied the same asset-capitalisation treatment to part (iii) as part (i), not recognising that Para 46A's asset-linked capitalisation route is only available when the borrowing financed a depreciable asset; where it instead financed operations, the FCMITD accumulation-and-amortisation route applies.

PYQ November 2023 · Q1(b) · Marks: 5 · Topic 3.3/3.4/3.5: Trade payable/receivable restated at closing rate vs. a non-monetary asset (plant, settled same day) held at transaction-date rate; exchange gain/loss recognised on each outstanding monetary item
Author’s Note: Many examinees correctly applied the closing rate to the trade receivable and trade payable but incorrectly restated the plant and machinery – a non-monetary item already settled in cash on the date of import – to the 31st March closing rate as well, not recognising that AS 11 requires non-monetary items carried at historical cost to remain at the transaction-date rate. Some examinees also computed the exchange gain/loss by comparing the transaction-date rupee value to the closing-rate rupee value directly rather than isolating the per-unit rate movement on the outstanding foreign-currency amount, occasionally producing the correct final figure by an incorrect method.

Author’s Note: A common error is adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the exchange difference between the transaction-date and settlement-date rates, missing that AS 11 requires monetary items to be restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date, with the resulting exchange difference recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss, not adjusted against the non-monetary cost of raw material already recorded.

My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
PYQ May 2024 · Q3(a) · Marks: 7 · Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion via costs-incurred-to-date/total-estimated-costs, revision of contract price and cost estimates mid-contract (change in estimate), profit recognised as revenue less cost incurred each year
Examiner’s Comment: Most examinees showed a lack of knowledge of the provisions of AS 7 Construction Contracts. They were required to calculate the percentage of stage of completion for each of the four years. While many did this correctly, some made errors in Year 1 by not considering the revised estimated expenditure, leading to incorrect percentages. A few examinees calculated the percentage completion for each year instead of the stage of completion and failed to calculate the profit to be recognized each year. Some mistook contract revenue for contract profit, and others incorrectly used cumulative figures to determine annual profit without separately calculating contract revenue and contract cost for each year.

Author’s Note: A frequent slip is treating the entire ₹16,00,000 grant as available to write down the asset's book value below zero, without recognising that once the asset's book value is reduced to nil, the excess grant amount must instead be recognised as income (a partial recovery of the depreciation already charged in earlier years) rather than left as a negative asset balance.

Author’s Note: A common error is writing the refund entry entirely against the Deferred Grant Account balance without recognising that only ₹16 lakhs remains there after two years' amortisation, forcing the shortfall of ₹16 lakhs to be debited to Profit and Loss; a related error is reducing the fixed asset's own book value on refund, when AS 12 requires the asset's carrying amount and future depreciation to continue unchanged since the grant was never netted against the asset's cost under the deferred-income method.

Author’s Note: A common error here is treating any book-tax gap as a timing difference by default; only differences capable of reversing in a future period (like depreciation) are timing differences, while items that never reverse (like a permanently tax-exempt income) are permanent differences and never generate deferred tax.

Author’s Note: Several examinees agreed with the accountant's policy of capitalising repairs and maintenance merely because it had been disclosed as an accounting policy, not recognising that disclosure under AS 1 cannot cure a treatment that is otherwise incorrect.

My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP November 2023 Set 2 · Q1(d) · Marks: 5 · Topic n/a: Fundamental accounting assumptions (Going Concern, Consistency, Accrual) presumed and not usually separately disclosed unless not followed; disclosure of all significant accounting policies at one place; disclosure of material changes in accounting policy including where the effect is not ascertainable
Author’s Note: A common error is inverting statements (i) and (ii), reasoning that fundamental accounting assumptions must be specifically stated precisely because they are so foundational, when AS 1's actual rule is the opposite – they are presumed and go unstated unless departed from, at which point disclosure becomes mandatory.

Author’s Note: A common error here is classifying every deposit or advance strictly by its own maturity date without considering the "held for use in normal operating cycle" test that Schedule III applies alongside the 12-month rule for genuinely operational items like the electricity security deposit.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
PYQ January 2025 · Q6(a) [OR-alt 2] · Marks: 4 · Topic unindexed: Going concern fundamental accounting assumption - when an entity is not a going concern, assets/liabilities are stated on a realisable-value basis rather than historical cost
Author’s Note: Some examinees prepared this Profit & Loss Account on the usual historical-cost/going-concern basis, missing that the firm's planned shutdown from 1st April, 2024 required Machinery and Closing Stock to be restated to realisable value rather than carried at cost or the lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule used for an ongoing business.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
PYQ May 2023 · Q6(a) · Marks: 5 · Topic n/a: Substance over form, fundamental accounting assumptions (accrual), and disclosure not being a remedy for non-compliance
Author’s Note: A number of examinees, when asked to comment on the AS 1 disclosure scenarios, incorrectly concluded that disclosing a departure from a specific standard such as AS 2 in the notes cures the non-compliance and preserves a true-and-fair view, not recognising that AS 1 disclosure is a transparency requirement and never a substitute for correct accounting treatment. Some also failed to identify that accounting policy disclosure belongs in the financial statements themselves, not the Directors' Report.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
PYQ November 2023 · Q5(b) · Marks: 5 · Topic unindexed: Disclosure requirements across four illustrations: a sub-probable contingent loss, mis-stated capitalisation policy disclosed rather than corrected, disclosure of a followed fundamental accounting assumption, and disclosure of a material accounting-policy change
Author’s Note: Some examinees, in part (i), incorrectly concluded that disclosing the probable loss in the financial statements was sufficient without first questioning whether a provision should have been recognised at all, given the disputed suit had only a 25% probability of being lost. In part (ii), several examinees accepted the chief accountant's own disclosure of the wrong capitalisation policy as adequate compliance, missing AS 1's rule that disclosure is never a substitute for correcting a treatment that is itself wrong. In part (iv), many examinees failed to recognise that a material change expected to affect future periods still requires disclosure of the change and its effect, even though no restatement of prior years was needed.

MTP January 2025 Set 1 · Q5 · Marks: 14 · Topic 1.17: Restating a subsidiary's balance sheet to uniform accounting policies (inventory method, doubtful-debt provision rate, deferred-expenditure write-off period) before consolidation
Author’s Note: A recurring error is adjusting only the inventory-valuation difference for uniform accounting policies while forgetting that the doubtful-debts provision rate and the deferred sales-promotion write-off period also need to be restated to the parent's policy before consolidation.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q2(a) · Marks: 7 · Topic 1.11: Cost of control - goodwill/capital reserve against revalued net assets, net of pre-acquisition dividend
Author’s Note: A common error is comparing the cost of investment against the subsidiary's unrevalued net assets, or failing to net the pre-acquisition dividend against the cost of investment before computing goodwill or capital reserve.

MTP January 2025 Set 2 · Q2(b) · Marks: 7 · Topic 1.12: Minority interest computed separately at acquisition date and at consolidation date across five cases
Author’s Note: A common error is computing minority interest only at the date of acquisition and not separately recomputing it at the date of consolidation using the later Share Capital and Profit & Loss balances, since the minority's proportionate share of accumulated profits changes between the two dates even where share capital does not.
Student Self Notes:
My NB Page No   My Tag   Revision Phase 1 2 3
MTP January 2026 Set 1 · Q3 · Marks: 14 · Topic 1.9: Minority interest turning negative - losses absorbed by holding company, recouped from future minority profits
Author’s Note: A very common error across multiple sittings on this exact pattern: continuing to show a negative (debit) minority interest balance in the consolidated balance sheet, instead of transferring the excess loss to the holding company (Cost of Control) and recouping it against the minority's later profit shares before crediting minority interest again.

MTP May 2024 Set 1 · Q5 · Marks: 14 · Topic 1.11/1.12: First-consolidation goodwill/capital-reserve computation and minority interest, where the subsidiary was held since incorporation (no pre-acquisition reserve split needed)
Author’s Note: A common error is splitting Anushka Ltd.'s general reserve into pre- and post-acquisition portions by default, without recognising that since Virat Ltd. held its stake from Anushka's very incorporation, the entire reserve balance is necessarily post-acquisition (revenue) profit, with no capital-profit component.

MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q5(a) · Marks: 7 · Topic 1.11: Goodwill/Capital Reserve computed against revalued net assets, cost of investment reduced by pre-acquisition dividend received
Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the parent's share of net assets against the unrevalued figures given in the balance sheet, or forgetting to reduce the cost of investment by the pre-acquisition dividend received before comparing it against the share of net assets.

MTP May 2024 Set 2 · Q5(b) · Marks: 7 · Topic 1.14: Revaluation of a subsidiary's asset on acquisition, split between capital (pre-acquisition) profit and post-acquisition additional depreciation
Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the additional depreciation on the revalued asset for the full year rather than only the post-acquisition 6-month period (1 October 2023 to 31 March 2024), or forgetting to net off the depreciation already charged on the original book value before arriving at the incremental amount.

MTP May 2025 Set 1 · Q2 · Marks: 14 · Topic 1.11/1.12/1.14: Cost of control/goodwill, minority interest, and asset revaluation with short-depreciation adjustment on a partly-owned subsidiary
Author’s Note: A common error is treating the equipment revaluation entirely as a post-acquisition (revenue) item since it was recorded by P Ltd. rather than in Q Ltd.'s own books, missing that the revaluation relates to the asset's value at the 1 April 2023 acquisition date and is therefore a capital profit, while only the resulting short depreciation for the year is a revenue item.

Author’s Note: A common error is defaulting to labelling the difference "Goodwill" without checking its sign — here the cost of acquisition is lower than the proportionate share of net assets acquired, so the difference is a Capital Reserve, the reverse of the more commonly tested Goodwill case.

Author’s Note: A frequent mistake in this kind of multi-year problem is letting the Minority Interest balance go negative when losses exceed it, instead of capping it at nil and tracking the excess as a memorandum recoverable from the minority's own future profits before any new profit share is credited to Minority Interest.

Author’s Note: A common error is computing goodwill on the associate's acquisition as a single blended calculation across both tranches, missing that AS 23 requires each tranche of investment to be compared against the investee's net asset value at that tranche's own acquisition date, since intervening changes in net assets affect the goodwill computed on the later tranche.

About the Author

CA Pranav Pratik Tulshyan holds All India Rank 1 in both Foundation (188/200, January 2015) and Intermediate (544/700, February 2016): the only student in the 70-year history of ICAI to achieve this from outside India, across both examinations. He holds AIR 5 in CA Finals. He completed his articleship at Ernst & Young, Gurgaon, and has worked across IOCL and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Government of India. He now teaches CA Inter Accounts at VC Gurukul, Noida.

This Amritras was built the same way his Advanced Accounts classes are taught: every question placed exactly where it belongs, nothing left to guesswork about what's actually been examined.

A Closing Note

This is the first edition of this Amritras — the distilled companion to the full Question Bank Book, meant for the final stretch before your exam, when you need the coordinates of every question and its one key insight, not the whole worked solution again.

For the complete book with the full question and worked answer, visit vcgurukul.com. If you found an error, or a question that's misfiled, or a topic tag that looks wrong, the single most useful thing you can do is email capranavpratiktulshyan@gmail.com with the question reference.

Good luck with your attempt.
